section_summary: This section opens with a 1942 League of Nations circular transmitting Bechuanaland Protectorate’s annual narcotics report for 1941. Most of the section concerns Taiwan under Japanese rule: a 1930 American consular survey of the controversial opium-licensing system, petitions opposing that system, and a physicians’ memorial advocating treatment rather than new licenses. It concludes with a lengthy Government-General publication defending gradual suppression, presenting statistics and administrative controls, and reproducing the revised Opium Ordinance and related regulations.

subfiles.title: Annual Reports by Governments for 1941: Bechuanaland Protectorate—Traffic in Opium and Other Dangerous Drugs
subfiles.doc_type: League of Nations circular and annual government report
subfiles.from: Acting Secretary-General of the League of Nations, communicating a United Kingdom report signed by J. W. Stirling
subfiles.to: League of Nations Council and members, parties to the 1931 Convention, and the Advisory Committee on Traffic in Opium and Other Dangerous Drugs
subfiles.about: Transmits Bechuanaland Protectorate’s annual report on narcotics administration and enforcement during 1941.
subfiles.summary: The report states that narcotics laws and administration were unchanged and that the import-certificate system worked satisfactorily. It reports no illicit traffic, production of raw opium or coca, or manufacture of drugs. Indian hemp or “dagga” was indigenous and illicitly smoked in small quantities, producing twenty-one possession convictions, while drug permits were confined to medical practitioners and government veterinary officers.

subfiles.title: A Survey of the Opium Situation in Taiwan
subfiles.doc_type: United States consular survey or report
subfiles.from: Vice Consul Charles S. Reed II, Taihoku, Taiwan
subfiles.to: United States Embassy and Consulate General in Tokyo and the Department of State
subfiles.about: Examines the Taiwan Government-General’s opium-licensing policy, public opposition, smuggling, and the visit of a League of Nations commission.
subfiles.summary: The report describes controversy over plans to license tens of thousands of previously clandestine smokers and contrasts official claims of gradual suppression with criticism from the Formosan Social Democratic Party. It recounts the League commission’s visit, speeches by Japanese officials, and interviews with both opponents and supporters of the policy. The author concludes that government administration had failed to control smoking and smuggling, discusses cocaine and possible morphine production, and recommends a specialized narcotics bureau.

subfiles.title: The Petition Regarding the Question of Opium Monopolization
subfiles.from: Taiwan Minshu To (Formosan Social Democratic Party)
subfiles.about: Petitions the League of Nations to oppose Taiwan’s opium monopoly and the proposed licensing of additional smokers.
subfiles.summary: The petition charges that the Japanese colonial government maintained the opium-licensing system to preserve monopoly revenue rather than protect public health. Tables compare the number of licensed smokers and annual monopoly income from 1897 through 1928, with the party arguing that price increases kept revenue high despite declining registrations. It characterizes new licenses as contrary to humanity and international obligations and asks the League to support abolition of special permission to smoke opium.

subfiles.title: Explanatory Note and Memorial Regarding Special Permission for New Opium-Smoking Licenses
subfiles.about: Explains official obstruction of a physicians’ memorial and presents their medical objections to granting new opium licenses.
subfiles.summary: The explanatory note says the Higher Police Department prevented submission of the memorial, interfered with the physicians’ meeting, and threatened restrictions on the Formosan press. The memorial argues that habitual smokers can be treated medically and that licensing former secret smokers would damage public health and frustrate suppression efforts. It recommends education, public-health propaganda, a declared end to licensing, support for treatment hospitals, specialist departments in government hospitals, and closer medical supervision of existing smokers.

subfiles.title: Opium System and Control of Narcotic Drugs in Formosa (Taiwan), Japan
subfiles.doc_type: Government publication with statistical tables and annexed laws and regulations
subfiles.to: General public and the Commission of Enquiry into the Control of Opium Smoking in the Far East
subfiles.about: Defends Taiwan’s gradual-suppression policy and details the administration, statistics, and law governing opium and smoking implements.
subfiles.summary: The publication traces the opium monopoly and licensing system from 1896 through the revised 1929 ordinance, presenting it as a humanitarian program of gradual suppression. Extensive tables cover licensed smokers by sex, age, and nationality; opium sales, imports, manufacture, and licensed businesses; smuggling cases; and prosecutions for clandestine smoking. It explains rationing, wholesale and retail controls, police and customs enforcement, and common smuggling methods. The annex reproduces the revised Opium Ordinance and enforcement provisions on licensing, possession, imports, penalties, medicinal opium, smoking implements, and recordkeeping; the text continues beyond page 62.
